target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would reliably remove voting barriers by giving people time off from work and school.
objection: A federal holiday would not require private employers to give paid time off, so many low-income workers in retail, food service, and gig work may still have to work or lose wages; therefore the scheduling-barrier argument does not reliably help the people most constrained.

target: AG1’s assumption that an Election Day holiday is an effective way to increase turnout.
objection: Making Election Day a holiday by itself is not a proven turnout strategy and is less reliable than targeted voting-access reforms such as employer time-to-vote laws, early/absentee/mail voting, lower-friction registration, and automatic voter registration.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday fails because it does not guarantee paid leave for low-wage workers.
objection: Even without a paid-leave mandate, a federal holiday typically changes real-world logistics: more businesses close or reduce hours, public institutions and childcare arrangements become more available, and employers are less likely to force workers to choose between wages and voting time.

target: AG2’s claim that other reforms are better because they are more direct and evidence-aligned than a holiday.
objection: A holiday is not meant to be the only reform; it can work alongside early voting, easier registration, and time-to-vote protections, while directly addressing the common problem that standard work and school hours conflict with voting day.

target: AG1’s idea that changing schedules around Election Day will meaningfully help low-income workers.
objection: Retail, service, and other lower-wage jobs frequently remain open even on holidays, so workers can still be scheduled to cover Election Day and remain stuck with the same wages-versus-voting tradeoff.

target: AG1’s assumption that a holiday reduces the need to request time off and therefore solves the access problem.
objection: For low-income workers, the real bottleneck is whether they can vote without losing income, not merely whether schedules are more flexible; without a requirement for paid time to vote, a holiday can benefit flexible workers more than those who are least able to lose wages.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday remains valuable even if paired with other reforms.
objection: If time-to-vote protections are the real solution, then an Election Day holiday becomes an extra, costly, and uncertain layer rather than the main mechanism, so policymakers should enact the direct employer-facing rules instead of relying on the holiday.

target: AG2’s claim that time-to-vote protections make a holiday redundant.
objection: A holiday and time-to-vote protections are complementary rather than redundant: the holiday reduces how much time people need by shifting the surrounding schedule, while the protections address whether people can take that time without losing income.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is unreliable because employers and institutions can ignore it.
objection: A national holiday sets a common public baseline that affects institutions beyond any single employer, and unlike state rules, it is uniform nationwide rather than varying in strength or enforcement from place to place.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday would broadly ease voting logistics.
objection: If schools or daycare close but employers still require coverage, parents may face new wages-versus-childcare tradeoffs; a holiday does not include childcare subsidies or paid leave, so it can add costs rather than remove them for low-income workers.

target: AG1’s assertion that a holiday is additive and therefore worth adopting even if other reforms are still needed.
objection: Politically, once Election Day becomes a holiday, lawmakers and employers may treat the problem as solved and stop pushing the stronger wage-protection and time-to-vote reforms, so the holiday can distract from the real constraint.

target: AG1’s claim that pairing a holiday with time-to-vote rules solves the low-income worker problem.
objection: If the holiday only becomes fair when added to enforceable time-to-vote protections, then the protections—not the holiday—are doing the real work, and the holiday is merely a symbolic calendar change that risks delaying or crowding out better reforms.

target: AG1’s argument that the holiday should be pursued as part of a broader package.
objection: There is an opportunity-cost problem: passing a national holiday requires major federal legislation and political capital that could instead be used for faster, enforceable state or local steps like paid or protected time to vote and automatic registration, and research suggests a holiday by itself does not outperform those reforms.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday is independently useful because it sets a predictable nationwide calendar baseline.
objection: If enforceable time-to-vote protections are still needed to prevent wage loss, then those protections are the main lever and the holiday adds little marginal benefit while still carrying costs and political tradeoffs; state-level direct access reforms address the decisive constraint more directly.
